candidates.name: HowTheyVote/data
candidates.what_it_holds: Weekly-updated CSV.gz exports (votes.csv.gz, plus MEP and political-group tables) of every roll-call vote in the European Parliament, collected by howtheyvote.eu; downloadable via GitHub releases as a single export.zip, with pandas-ready examples in the README. 121 commits, actively maintained (weekly cadence).
candidates.why_useful: Machine-readable, point-in-time (weekly snapshot) EU Parliament vote history could locate/timestamp any EU-level short-term-rental or platform-economy (DAC7-adjacent) votes relevant to gap #12 (EU regulation trackers) and is a clean template for a point-in-time EU political-risk series (gap #4 vintage angle).
candidates.time_coverage: rolling, updated weekly (start year not confirmed from fetch)
candidates.size_hint: csv.gz export + full export.zip, row counts not confirmed
candidates.last_activity: actively maintained, weekly updates per README

candidates.name: parltrack/parltrack
candidates.what_it_holds: Scraper + application ('Parliamentary Tracker') that builds a queryable database of European Parliament dossiers, votes, and MEP activity from EP sources; 639 commits, 74 stars. Page did not expose committed data dumps directly but the project is known to publish periodic JSON/DB dumps via parltrack.org.
candidates.why_useful: A second, older/broader EU legislative-tracking tool than HowTheyVote; could be used to pull the legislative history of any EU platform-economy/short-term-rental dossier (gap #12) with dated snapshots (gap #4).
candidates.last_activity: not confirmed (639 commits total, appears maintained)

candidates.name: openstates/openstates-scrapers
candidates.what_it_holds: Open States project's scraper codebase (22,236 commits, GPL-3.0, actively maintained) covering bills and votes for all 50 US state legislatures, feeding the Open States API/bulk data. Not itself a committed bill-text dataset here, but the live method to pull every state-level short-term-rental bill (registration caps, tax changes, statewide preemption fights) with bill status history.
candidates.why_useful: Fills gap #12 (STR ordinance/legislation trackers) at the state level across all 50 states, complementing city-level Legistar coverage; state preemption laws are a first-order driver of city STR caps that affect Airbnb US supply.
candidates.time_coverage: ongoing, current legislative sessions (historical depth varies by state)
candidates.size_hint: very large scraper codebase; underlying Open States API/bulk data separately hosted

candidates.name: opencivicdata/python-legistar-scraper
candidates.what_it_holds: Generic Python library (707 commits) for scraping any city's Legistar-hosted legislative site (agendas, matters/ordinances, votes, people) into a normalized structure; used as the base library by DataMade's municipal scrapers.
candidates.why_useful: The core reusable client needed to pull city-council STR ordinance histories (hearing dates, vote counts, bill text links) for any of the ~40+ US cities that run Legistar (LA, SF, Boston, Chicago, Nashville, New Orleans, Austin, Denver, etc.) named in gap #12; complements the municipal registries we already hold with the legislative *process* record (when caps/bans were debated and passed).
candidates.time_coverage: as far back as each city's Legistar instance retains records (often 2000s-present)

candidates.name: datamade/scrapers-us-municipal
candidates.what_it_holds: DataMade's fork/production deployment (1,680 commits, MIT license) of the Legistar-based municipal scraper covering Chicago, Cook County, Ferguson, LA Metro, Miami-Dade, New York City, Pittsburgh, Sacramento, and St. Louis city councils, feeding ocd.datamade.us.
candidates.why_useful: Ready-configured scrapers for several cities already in our STR panel (NYC, LA-area via LA Metro, Chicago) to pull the underlying council legislative record (ordinance introduction/vote dates) around STR regulation, useful as a companion to the registry data we already hold.
candidates.geography: Chicago, Cook County, Ferguson MO, LA Metro, Miami-Dade, NYC, Pittsburgh, Sacramento, St. Louis

candidates.name: c-tonneslan/convene
candidates.what_it_holds: Python tool (MIT, 12 commits) that pulls municipal meeting data via the Legistar Web API and Granicus scraping into a normalized OCD-shaped JSON/NDJSON/CSV/iCal output, preconfigured for 24 US cities including Philadelphia, NYC, Chicago, Seattle, San Francisco, Denver, and Boston; outputs meetings, legislation with sponsors, vote records and action histories, with worked JSON examples in the README.
candidates.why_useful: Lightweight, easy one-command client to pull council-level ordinance/vote histories for STR-relevant cities (SF OSTR, NYC, Denver, Boston) — a smaller, more approachable alternative to the DataMade/opencivicdata stack for gap #12.
candidates.time_coverage: current + historical depending on city's Legistar/Granicus retention
candidates.geography: 24 preconfigured US cities (Philadelphia, NYC, Chicago, Seattle, SF, Denver, Boston, others)
candidates.size_hint: code + README examples only, no bulk committed data

candidates.name: timmKal01/city-council-watch
candidates.what_it_holds: Apify actor (3 commits) that fetches newly filed ordinances/resolutions and upcoming council/committee agendas from any city's Legistar Web API given a city code as a parameter; no hardcoded city list or committed data, source/config/Dockerfile only.
candidates.why_useful: A generic, parameterizable way to monitor new STR-ordinance filings in near-real time across any Legistar city, which could catch new caps/bans as they are introduced ahead of the pitch deadline (gap #12); marginal given its small size and lack of committed data.
candidates.time_coverage: forward-looking only (new filings since a given date)

candidates.name: freelawproject/courtlistener
candidates.what_it_holds: The full open-source codebase (25,363 commits, AGPL license) behind CourtListener.com, Free Law Project's searchable archive of federal/state court opinions, oral arguments, judges, and (via RECAP) federal docket filings; the live site and its API/bulk-data exports (not directly confirmed in this fetch, but documented at wiki.free.law) can be queried for Airbnb Inc. litigation (e.g. host/guest class actions, city-vs-Airbnb regulatory suits, IP/antitrust cases) with case metadata and filing dates.
candidates.why_useful: The best free method to build a point-in-time litigation docket for Airbnb (host lawsuits, city STR-ordinance enforcement suits, DOJ/FTC matters) that could carry event-study/regulatory-risk signal for gap #12 and the events/shocks gap (#11); the codebase itself is not a dataset but confirms the underlying API/bulk data exist to query.
candidates.time_coverage: federal courts back to ~1600s for some opinions per site; RECAP dockets from ~2009-present
candidates.size_hint: 9M+ opinions per topic-page description; codebase itself large (25k+ commits)
candidates.last_activity: actively maintained (937 open issues, ongoing commits)

candidates.name: freelawproject/recap (recap-chrome)
candidates.what_it_holds: Issue tracker for RECAP, a crowdsourced Chrome/Firefox extension (main code in freelawproject/recap-chrome, 550 commits) that captures and re-shares PACER federal court filings for free, feeding into the CourtListener/RECAP archive.
candidates.why_useful: Complementary tooling to CourtListener for finding and archiving PACER filings in any active Airbnb federal litigation (e.g. host classification suits, regulatory challenges) without paying PACER fees; same gap targets as CourtListener above.

candidates.name: courtlistener-api-client (search-yourself, ~28 stars)
candidates.what_it_holds: A third-party Python SDK for CourtListener's REST API, letting a script query case law and court opinions programmatically (no data committed in the repo itself).
candidates.why_useful: A lighter-weight alternative to writing raw HTTP calls against CourtListener's API to pull Airbnb-related case law/dockets on demand; convenience method only, no unique data.

candidates.name: CouncilDataProject (org: cdp-backend, cdp-scrapers, speakerbox, and per-city repos)
candidates.what_it_holds: A 'search engine for local government' spanning 18+ US municipalities (Seattle, Denver, Oakland, Charlotte, Milwaukee, Boston, Pittsburgh, Atlanta, others), combining city-council meeting video/audio transcription (speakerbox), a scraping pipeline (cdp-scrapers), and a searchable backend (cdp-backend, MPL-2.0) that stores meeting minutes, agenda items, and vote records per city, each in its own per-city GitHub/cloud-hosted deployment.
candidates.why_useful: Deeper than plain Legistar scraping: full-text-searchable council meeting transcripts could surface STR-ordinance debates, votes, and public comment in cities we already track (Seattle, Boston, Pittsburgh) or add new ones, feeding gap #12 with qualitative/timestamped regulatory-process detail rather than just bill metadata.
candidates.geography: 18+ US cities (Seattle, Denver, Oakland, Charlotte, Milwaukee, Boston, Pittsburgh, Atlanta, others)
candidates.size_hint: distributed across per-city cloud-hosted databases + GitHub org repos; not a single flat file
candidates.last_activity: not confirmed, org appears active with multiple maintained sub-repos

notes: Both WebSearch (session-wide budget exhausted before this scout's first query) and github.com/search (429 rate-limited, retry-after 3600s, evidently exhausted by other concurrent scouts hitting the same GitHub search endpoint) were unavailable for the entire run. DuckDuckGo HTML search returned only a CAPTCHA wall. Bing search pages, when fetched, did not surface usable GitHub-specific results through the WebFetch summarizer (it appears to summarize an unrelated cached/JS-rendered version of the SERP rather than true site: results). Worked around by: (1) WebFetch on individual github.com/<owner>/<repo> pages guessed from domain knowledge, and (2) WebFetch on github.com/topics/<tag> pages, both of which loaded normally (no 429) and were more reliable than search. This means the sweep is materially narrower than intended (no true full-text search of GitHub or the open web was possible) — a rerun once the WebSearch budget resets or the GitHub search rate limit clears would likely surface more STR-ordinance-specific repos (e.g. city open-data-portal mirrors of SF OSTR/LA HSO permit rosters, academic replication packages for STR-regulation-effect papers, and dedicated 'airbnb ban tracker' community projects) that a keyword search would find but individual-page guessing cannot. The 'airbnb-regulation' and 'dac7' GitHub topic tags are confirmed literally unused (zero repos), so any relevant repos there are untagged and only findable via full-text/code search. Flag for a follow-up scout once search tooling is available: Harvard Dataverse / SSRN-linked GitHub replication packages for STR-regulation-effect economics papers (e.g. work following Barron/Kung/Proserpio-style natural experiments), and city open-data-portal (Socrata/CKAN) mirrors of short-term-rental permit/enforcement data that sit alongside legislative trackers.
queries_run_count_note: 16 distinct search attempts (all search-engine-based ones failed/blocked) plus ~19 targeted WebFetch verification calls on individual repos/topic pages.
